messages:
mira: ran an nsys capture on replica-3 under a steady 200 qps synthetic scenario. seeing a weird distribution where two small kernels (kv_read_cuda and kv_evict_cuda) collectively consume most of the wall time during certain intervals. pasted top kernels below from the capture summary.

mira: ```
Top CUDA kernels by total time (nsys summary):
1) kv_read_cuda          39.8% (1.56s)
2) dispatch_attention   16.3% (0.64s)
3) kv_evict_cuda        11.7% (0.46s)
4) aten::matmul_cu       8.9% (0.35s)
5) softmax_fwd           5.4% (0.19s)
others                  17.9%
```

devon: that's pretty high for kv_read. did you capture kernel launch counts / per-launch latencies?

mira: yes - nvprof-style counters show ~120k launches of kv_read_cuda across the 30s trace. per-launch median ~9.8us, p95 ~18us. grid/block config is small: block=128 threads, grid=48 in most launches. occupancy snapshot shows active warps often in the single-digit range.

sam: single-digit active warps == terrible occupancy. that plus lots of tiny launches will create SM thrashing and high launch overhead. any memcpy patterns around kv_evict?

mira: perfetto timeline shows memcpy_async bursts immediately before kv_evict ranges; some memcpy windows align with host->device copy of eviction metadata. Also noticed cudaStreamSynchronize calls occasionally from the eviction path (likely to ensure ordering).

aaron: two likely levers: (1) our reduced batching.threshold_ms in the last rollout (we moved threshold_ms 1.5 -> 0.7 to reduce tail latency) which reduced aggregation and increased small-batch churn, and (2) eviction path doing synchronous handoffs causing short gaps and memcpy bursts.

devon: agreed. timeline (SM util per 50ms buckets) looks like: [74, 69, 12, 9, 76, 71, 11, 8] with kv ops concentrated in the low-util buckets. classic microburst pattern.

mira: captured one representative launch profile for kv_read_cuda:
```
Kernel: kv_read_cuda
  block size: 128
  grid size: 48
  observed active warps: 4/32 -> 12.5%
  avg exec time: 10.2us (lots of repeats)
  registers per thread: 20
  shared mem per block: 256B
```

sam: registers/shmem don't look catastrophic, it's just the parallelism being too small per launch. we should examine whether we can batch multiple reads into a single kernel invocation or fuse evict+read where applicable.

mira: propose quick experiments (will run on prod-staging overnight):
- A: revert batching.threshold_ms to 1.6ms and capture same synthetic workload to see launch count and top-kernel shift
- B: keep threshold 0.7ms but enable kv_read_coalesce=true (runtime flag) which aggregates small reads in the driver into a single kernel call when possible
- C: instrument KV eviction to use cudaMemcpyAsync into a pinned staging buffer and avoid host syncs; also add NVTX ranges around KV ops to separate memcpy vs compute in traces
- D: try runtime.enable_kernel_grouping=1 to test kernel fusion for short-lived kernels (needs ABI check, might be flaky)

devon: +1 to A/B/C. D is high-risk but worth a short canary. also please include a run with nvtx emitting stream IDs so we can check whether launches go to the same stream or scatter across streams.

mira: will add NVTX and stream IDs. also noticed that when kv_evicts are frequent, the allocator churn increases (CUDA mem ops show many small frees/allocs). might be worth changing eviction to reuse a ring buffer for staging.

sam: good call. if we can reduce alloc/free in eviction we can avoid PCIe and CPU-side churn. also check whether TCP driver threads are pinning into the same CPU core and causing serialization before memcpy_async.

tracing-bot: nsys capture uploaded: https://artifacts.internal/redwood/nsys/replica3_2012345678_kv_thrash.ns (58.1MB) :spiral_note_pad:

mira: I'll run A/B/C overnight and post the new top-kernel tables + occupancy histograms tomorrow AM. tagging @devon @sam @aaron. :thumbsup:
